# howbig

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

**How big a sample do you need to find what changed in a network?**

howbig gives power and sample-size calculations for differential network
analysis: comparing two groups' Gaussian graphical models to find the edges
that differ. It is a network-native, method-aware analogue to
[pwr](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pwr).

Its answers are empirical. They come from a large simulation study that ran
seven estimation methods across sample sizes, feature counts, and kinds of
differential signal, plus an on-demand simulator for designs the study didn't
cover. That evidence shows things a formula would hide:

- **Required sample sizes are large.** With 250 features, the joint graphical
  lasso needs roughly 4,500 samples per group to recover 80% of the
  differential edges.
- **Method choice matters, and no method wins everywhere.**
- **Some methods lose FDR control under some kinds of signal.** howbig reports
  the false discovery rate a method actually achieves, next to its power, so
  that assumption is visible.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/howbig")
```

Looking up and interpolating the grid needs nothing else. To *simulate* a
method you also need its package; `dependencies = TRUE` installs them all
(several come from GitHub):

```r
remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/howbig", dependencies = TRUE)
```

## Example

You need four things: roughly how many features you'll measure (`p`), a
sample size per group (`n`), the method you plan to use, and what kind of
change you expect between groups.

```{r example}
library(howbig)

power_for(p = 250, n = 1000, method = "JGL_BIC")
```

*Power* here is **sensitivity**: the fraction of truly differential edges
detected while controlling the false discovery rate at 5%. To go the other
way, ask for the sample size that reaches a target power:

```{r}
n_for(p = 250, power = 0.8, method = "JGL_BIC")
```

If you expect edge **strengths** to change rather than edges to appear or
disappear, the picture changes. This method stops controlling its false
discovery rate:

```{r}
power_for(p = 250, n = 1000, method = "JGL_BIC", perturbation = "magnitude")
```

## How answers are produced

Every answer states where it came from:

| Provenance | Meaning | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| `in-grid` | A precomputed simulation cell (typically 100 replicates) | instant |
| `interpolated` | Between grid cells along a swept axis | instant |
| `simulated` | A fresh simulation of your exact design | minutes to hours |
| `OFF-GRID` | Not answerable from the grid; howbig says why | - |

Designs the grid doesn't cover are flagged, not guessed:

```{r}
power_for(p = 150, n = 1500, method = "JGL_BIC")
```

Rerunning with `simulate = TRUE` simulates that design, as do unequal group
sizes (`n = c(600, 1400)`) and FDR targets other than 5%. Each simulation
estimates its runtime before it starts and refuses to start runs longer than
`max_minutes`.
